en: Of singular form and terrible venom,
My mountain-lion father, Khan Manas,
His bulletproof armor billowing—
If only that destroyer had stood watching!
Then let these Jediger here
Have shamed the suffering warrior,
Have inflicted this disgrace,
And then taken his life!
Wearing a blue-lynx cap,
Wielding a mottled blue shield,
When ten thousand foes appeared before him,
He gave them no longer than meat takes to cook.
His eyes saw into the distance;
He stood alone and unmatched in every contest.
The consummate sage Bakay,
Our forefather, mighty as a hero—
Our poor uncle Bakay
Was not watching from the ridge.
So the treacherous Kanchoro
Did not then commit his outrage,
Nor did he take my life.
He knew seventy winding tongues;
He traveled roads that led toward death.
He whetted his eloquence,
And never shrank or stayed behind in war.
He spoke before the people;
No enemy who faced him prospered,
And never was his word in vain.
A six-month ordeal
He foresaw from afar.
Descendant of Kök-Terek,
Eloquent spokesman of gray-maned Manas,
Achybay, son of the Argyn khan—
If only that cunning man had stood watching!
Then let the Jediger
Have inflicted this disgrace!
Thick-armed and stone-hearted,
Stout and powerfully built,
A scabbardless sword at his waist,
Like a cloud returning with rain,
His wrath spread across his face.
He broke through seven lines and opened a road;
If seventy thousand foes came,
He charged alone into their midst.
Foremost among the sixty,
Fiercest of the falcons,
Best of the spearmen,
Best of the warriors,
Black steel was his blade—
Syrgak of my father Khan Manas.
At the sight of an enemy he readied himself,
And steeped his steel in blood.
Though countless thousands of foes came,
Even facing death, he never fled.
In the finest years of his strength,
He was Syrgak, warrior of Manas,
Agile as a sparrowhawk,
A star by which to steer in the heavens,
Companion to my father Almambet.
If only brave Syrgak had stood watching!
Then let black-hearted Kanchoro
Have inflicted this disgrace!
With a fierce cry and a shrill battle shout,
He never turned back from combat,
But faced the enemy head-on.
He dyed his spear dark with blood
And struck down the formidable.
Of noble, golden aspect,
The foremost champion of the Kyrgyz,
Chubak, son of Khan Akbaltay,
Was himself a lion.
He wore a blue, arrow-proof coat
And rode a dappled blue charger.
When ten thousand foes appeared before him,
He struck without blinking.
If only your gray-maned hero Chubak
Had stood openly watching!
Then let Kanchoro
Have inflicted this disgrace!
Er Shuutu, whose cap was broad as a roof flap,
And Yrchy-uul, son of Yraman,
All the falcon warriors,
And Kutubiy, blessed with good fortune—
Who cut off a head when told to take a cap,
Who spilled his own lifeblood when told to shed blood,
Who drank poison when told to drink water—
The truest of the valiant companions:
If only all those falcons
Had turned and stood watching!
Then let Kanchoro
And brave Kyyaz of the Jediger
Have inflicted this disgrace!
Only then let them have wrung out my wretched, screaming soul
And taken my life!
My strength is exhausted and my vigor gone;
I have no power left to fight,
And dark blood drains from my body.
All the Jediger came swarming;
My fly-like little soul was hard-pressed.
The settlement fled and scattered;
The hostile foe, like a dragon,
Appeared close before my eyes.
Jylgyn and Keng-Kol remained behind,
The Argyn and Kyrgyz peoples remained behind;
Now only the grave awaited Külchoro.
I have no swift steed to seize and mount,
No kinsman to look to,
No forest into which to flee,
And no brother to stand beside me.
Could fate grow as dark as this?
If I turned away and fled, damn it,
If only I had a thoroughbred beneath me,
If only I had my former strength,
Would I not draw a trail
Across the whole wide world
And make such sport as never before?
I have no charger to choose and mount,
No kinsman to be my companion.
Flames fill me within, embers cover me without;
My confidant and uncle is not here.
If poor old Bakay—
My uncle above all—should die,
And I, his wretched warrior, should die,
If the moon were veiled in darkness,
“What would the night become?”
What would become of Kanykey in her old age,
And of the wretched aged Bakay?
“What would their days become?
Bakay will be left without burial;
The stooping old and foolish young,
Left alive in this false world,
Will likewise remain unburied.”
So Külchoro pondered deeply,
Because of every enemy,
And because of his life held only in trust.
His wrathful kindred khans,
Those precious souls, could not be hidden.
Unable to find his bearings,
Unable to cross Keng-Kol,
Unable to reach Kara-Üngkür,
The Black Cave of the holy seer,
His fly-like soul screamed.
His whole body was wounded;
All his bones and joints
Were shattered and crumbling like sand.
His broad boots with crescent heels
Flapped about his feet;
His khan uncle’s gray cartridge pouch
Slapped against the hero.
His father’s long matchlock rifle
Gleamed in his hand.
He had no single charge left
To fire the matchlock
And make Kyyaz and Kanchoro
Turn their backs and fall.
A dreadful calamity, a black fate—
Külchoro had no strength left.
The wide world became narrow;
He longed even for enough saliva
To swallow once and sustain his life.
Külchoro, who had scorned even rich mutton,
Was in a wretched state to behold.
His joints loosened, his insides burned;
His strength failed and his eyes blazed.
He could not cross toward Küdür;
Over the lower slopes of Üch-Koshoy
The warrior could not pass, though he wailed.
Through Kara-Buura and Chatkal,
Through dark, lofty marshlands,
Your warrior could not make his way,
Nor could he reach that well-known place.
The soles of his feet were torn open;
His two legs, a warrior’s support,
Were flayed and failed beneath him.
The thick flesh of his heels,
Striking the stones, was worn away.
At Jalg yz-Terek and Chuk-Terek,
In the hollow of ridged Besh-Tash,
Along the Kan-Jayloo,
Amid rugged, marshy hills,
Where dense honeysuckle grew below,
Was Kök-Üngkür among the blue honeysuckle.
When he scattered his vast wealth,
And yesterday the poor lame smith
Fled there in misery,
This had been his place of refuge.
By the spring at Chybyrluu, flowing for a thousand years,
Was the Cave of Khan Bakay,
Where many people had gathered since ancient times.
Külchoro reached Kara-Üngkür
And fled inside, exhausted,
Helpless and drained of blood.
His strength failed and his eyes burned;
No part of his body remained whole.
Dark blood streamed from him
As he sheltered in Kara-Üngkür.
The world he saw became narrow;
Külchoro, who never lay idle in the horde,
Now lay helpless in that cave.
Having fled inside the cave,
He propped himself on his elbows and rested,
Dozing briefly and finding sleep.
He lay on his side and let his spirit recover,
Sleeping until his need was satisfied.
Then Külchoro said:
“I was a shapely gray ridge
No man or mighty enemy could cross;
I was a pale-gray mountain pass.
I was a pale-gray falcon
From which no bustard escaped.
Blazing and glowing like fire,
I used to carve up game and eat it.
While my lionhearted uncle lived,
I used to say, ‘What calamity could touch me?’
Now my whole body is wounded;
My hero is gone from over my head,
And I am left in mourning.
Bullets have torn my shoulder apart,
And the foe has defiled my person.
Kara-Üngkür, holy shrine of the seer,
Hear my sorrowful words;
Let your sacred power increase.
Father Kara-Üngkür, hide me.
Shelter this wretch who seeks refuge today;
Father Kara-Üngkür, hide me.
Today I was a lion, a gray-maned hero;
If you are my blessing, Kara-Üngkür,
Today I look to you for protection.
If you are my guardian, Kara-Üngkür,
Clasp me tightly to your breast;
Nurse and restore me, Kara-Üngkür.
Be a father to me today
And keep me safe, Kara-Üngkür.
Be a shelter today
For this poor, forsaken soul, Kara-Üngkür.
Hide your poor one within your breast today
And be my guardian, Kara-Üngkür.
Would that you opened
Your white-mottled canopy, Kara-Üngkür.
Why not press your wretched one
To your bosom today, Kara-Üngkür?
Dear Kara-Üngkür,
Nurse this poor soul.
Today all strength and vigor have left this forlorn man;
Dear Kara-Üngkür,
Be a mother and protect me.
Your wretched one has come seeking refuge;
Be fruitful and sustaining, Kara-Üngkür.
Let down milk and open your heart;
Be a mother, Kara-Üngkür.
Oh, beloved Almighty,
You made this the place where infidels were routed;
You poured forth your sacred power,
Yet brought death before my eyes.
Why have you reduced me to such misery?
I was a lion who strode forth proudly,
